nodes.label: The Mamluk Sultanate
nodes.full: The slave-soldier state that had ruled Egypt and Syria since 1250, whose defeat in 1516–17 ends this folio's prehistory — and whose military caste, culture and institutions revive under Ottoman rule.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mamluks-1250-1517 (The Mamluk Sultanate)

nodes.label: The Ottoman Empire
nodes.full: The empire ruled from Istanbul, of which Egypt was the richest province — sending tribute, provisioning the capital and the Holy Cities, and receiving governors, judges and garrison regiments.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule (2008)

nodes.label: The Wahhabi movement
nodes.full: The austere revivalist movement of Najd, allied with the Al Saud, which rejected the culture of shrines and Sufi orders and, in the 1800s, took the Hijaz from Ottoman-Egyptian control.
nodes.src: background — added on review; see the Arabia folios

nodes.label: Muhammad Ali and modern Egypt
nodes.full: The Ottoman officer who seized power in the chaos after the French left, destroyed the Mamluk beys, and founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt to 1953 — the start of the country's modern transformation.
nodes.src: background — added on review; belongs to the next folio; Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997)

nodes.label: Selim I conquers Egypt
nodes.full: Selim I's army, with its field artillery and arquebusiers, destroyed the Mamluk cavalry at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and again at al-Raydaniyya outside Cairo in January 1517. The last Mamluk sultan, Tuman Bay, was caught after weeks of street fighting and hanged at the Bab Zuwayla. Egypt, an independent sultanate for two and a half centuries, became a province of the Ottoman empire, and Selim took the guardianship of the Holy Cities and, in later tradition, the caliphal title.
nodes.src: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i' al-zuhur (an eyewitness). Michael Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule 1517–1798 (1992) pp.7–13; Benjamin Lellouch, Les Ottomans en Égypte: historiens et conquérants au XVIe siècle (2006).

nodes.label: Khayr Bey and the first governors
nodes.full: Selim left Egypt under Khayr Bey, the Mamluk governor of Aleppo whose defection had helped win Marj Dabiq, as the first Ottoman viceroy. Khayr Bey kept much of the Mamluk apparatus and many Mamluk officers in place while an Ottoman garrison and Ottoman fiscal officials were installed alongside them. The compromise — Ottoman sovereignty over a still-partly-Mamluk administration — set the pattern for the whole period.
nodes.src: Ibn Iyas; Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.14–17; P.M. Holt, Egypt and the Fertile Crescent 1516–1922 (1966) pp.45–50.

nodes.label: The Qanunname and the ordered eyalet
nodes.full: After the governor Ahmad Pasha revolted and briefly declared himself an independent sultan, the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha came in person and issued the Qanunname-i Misir — a detailed code fixing the governor's powers, the seven military corps and their pay, the fiscal districts and the annual tribute (irsaliyye) owed to Istanbul, and the provisioning of Mecca and Medina. It was the constitution of Ottoman Egypt, cited as authoritative down to Bonaparte.
nodes.src: Ömer Lütfi Barkan, XV ve XVI Asırlarda Osmanlı İmparatorluğunda Ziraî Ekonominin Hukukî ve Malî Esasları (1943) prints the qanunname. Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization and Development of Ottoman Egypt (1962).

nodes.label: The pashas fade
nodes.full: Ottoman governors were rotated through Egypt every year or two, and by the seventeenth century most could not control the entrenched military corps or the reviving Mamluk beys. The local soldiery took to deposing an unsatisfactory pasha by acclamation — 'casting him out' — and appointing an acting governor until Istanbul sent another. Real authority drained from the Citadel to the barracks and the great households.
nodes.src: Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.20–34; Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt: The Rise of the Qazdağlıs (1997) pp.7–16.

nodes.label: The Mamluk households return
nodes.full: The Mamluk system quietly reconstituted itself under Ottoman rule. Grandees — the beys who held the twenty-four sanjak commands — built up households (bayts) of imported Caucasian slave-soldiers trained and freed as before, competing for the key offices of shaykh al-balad (senior bey) and amir al-hajj (commander of the pilgrimage caravan). Two rival blocs, the Faqari and the Qasimi, structured the politics of the century.
nodes.src: Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt (1997); P.M. Holt, 'The Beylicate in Ottoman Egypt during the Seventeenth Century', BSOAS 24 (1961).

nodes.label: Ridwan Bey al-Faqari
nodes.full: Ridwan Bey held the office of amir al-hajj almost continuously for a quarter of a century, the most powerful figure in Egypt while a succession of pashas came and went. His Faqari household and the rival Qasimi bloc under Ali Bey dominated the middle of the century, and his ascendancy established the model that would run to 1798: a single great bey, backed by his own household troops, overshadowing the Ottoman governor.
nodes.src: P.M. Holt, 'The Career of Küçük Muhammad (1676–94)', BSOAS 26 (1963) and 'The Pattern of Egyptian Political History from 1517 to 1798', in Holt (ed.), Political and Social Change in Modern Egypt (1968).

nodes.label: The Qazdughli ascendancy
nodes.full: A household founded within the Janissary corps by an officer called Qazdughli grew, over two generations, to dominate both the corps and the beylicate, absorbing or destroying its rivals. In the 1740s and 1750s Ibrahim Kahya and Ridwan Kahya ran Egypt as a 'dual amirate'. When Ibrahim died his mamluks fought for the succession, and out of that contest rose Ali Bey al-Kabir.
nodes.src: Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt: The Rise of the Qazdağlıs (1997). Daniel Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.31–44.

nodes.label: Ali Bey al-Kabir
nodes.full: Ali Bey, a Qazdughli mamluk of Georgian origin, eliminated his rivals, made himself shaykh al-balad, and by 1768 was expelling Ottoman governors, withholding the tribute, and striking coins in his own name — the first ruler to detach Egypt from Istanbul since 1517. He annexed the Hijaz and, in 1770–71, sent his army under Abu al-Dhahab to take Damascus in league with the Galilee shaykh Zahir al-Umar and, at a distance, with Russia, then at war with the Ottomans.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar. Daniel Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt: A Study of the Regimes of 'Ali Bey al-Kabir and Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab, 1760–1775 (1981).

nodes.label: Abu al-Dhahab's betrayal
nodes.full: Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab, Ali Bey's chief lieutenant and freedman, abruptly abandoned the Syrian campaign in 1772, marched back on Cairo, and drove his master out. Ali Bey fled to Zahir al-Umar, returned in 1773 with a Russian squadron's help, was beaten at al-Salihiyya, captured, and died of his wounds. Abu al-Dhahab then ruled as shaykh al-balad, made peace with Istanbul, invaded Syria on the sultan's behalf, and died before Acre in 1775.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar; Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981).

nodes.label: Ibrahim Bey and Murad Bey
nodes.full: For the last quarter-century of Ottoman Egypt two of Abu al-Dhahab's freedmen, Ibrahim Bey the administrator and Murad Bey the soldier, ruled jointly — feuding, splitting the country between them, and squeezing it with new taxes and confiscations. An Ottoman expedition under Hasan Pasha drove them to Upper Egypt in 1786, but they were back within two years. Their army, still built around lance and sabre, was destroyed by Bonaparte's infantry squares at Imbaba in 1798.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar; P.M. Holt, Egypt and the Fertile Crescent (1966) pp.85–100. The 1786 expedition: Stanford Shaw, Between Old and New: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim III (1971).

nodes.label: The French invasion
nodes.full: Bonaparte landed near Alexandria on 1 July 1798, beat the Mamluk cavalry at Imbaba across the Nile from Cairo on 21 July, and occupied the country for the French Directory, bringing 150-odd scholars and scientists whose survey became the Description de l'Égypte. Nelson destroyed the French fleet at Aboukir on 1 August, stranding the army; a Cairo uprising in October was put down with a bombardment of al-Azhar; and after Bonaparte slipped away, the occupation collapsed under a British and Ottoman assault in 1801.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, three accounts of the French occupation (translated Moreh, Napoleon in Egypt, 1993). Henry Laurens, L'expédition d'Égypte 1798–1801 (1989); Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007).

nodes.label: The military corps as a power
nodes.full: Seven Ottoman regiments garrisoned Egypt, the most important the Janissaries (Mustahfizan) and the Azaban. Beyond soldiering they controlled lucrative revenues — the customs of the ports, the mints, market and protection dues — recruited local men and merchants into their ranks, and repeatedly deposed pashas and fought the beys. Over the eighteenth century the leading households and the corps effectively merged, and the corps as an independent force faded into the Mamluk world.
nodes.src: Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt (1997) pp.17–51; André Raymond, 'Soldiers in Trade: The Case of Ottoman Cairo', British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies 18 (1991).

nodes.label: The Coptic patriarch and the archons
nodes.full: The Coptic patriarch, resident in Cairo, remained the head of the Christian community, a shrinking minority now but with a rising lay elite: the archons (arakhina), Coptic scribes, accountants and financiers indispensable to the tax administration and the Mamluk households. By the late eighteenth century Ibrahim al-Jawhari, a Copt, was in effect the chief financial officer of the whole regime, and his family endowed churches and monasteries on a scale not seen for centuries.
nodes.src: Magdi Guirguis & Nelly van Doorn-Harder, The Emergence of the Modern Coptic Papacy (2011); Magdi Guirguis, An Armenian Artist in Ottoman Egypt: Yuhanna al-Armani and His Coptic Icons (2008). On the Jawharis: al-Jabarti.

nodes.label: Marj Dabiq and al-Raydaniyya
nodes.full: The Mamluk state, still fighting on horseback with lance and bow and distrustful of the firearm, met an Ottoman army that used massed field guns and janissary muskets from behind a wagon-fort. At Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo in August 1516 the Mamluk sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri was killed and his army broken; at al-Raydaniyya outside Cairo in January 1517 the new sultan Tuman Bay's guns were outmanoeuvred. After days of street fighting he was betrayed, captured and hanged at the Bab Zuwayla.
nodes.src: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i' al-zuhur (eyewitness). Robert Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986); David Ayalon, Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom (1956).

nodes.label: Ahmad Pasha the Traitor
nodes.full: Ahmad Pasha, sent as governor after being passed over for grand vizier, seized the Citadel, minted coins, had the Friday sermon read in his own name, and proclaimed himself an independent sultan of Egypt — barely seven years into Ottoman rule. Loyal officers killed him in his bath within months. The revolt prompted Istanbul to send the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha to reorganise the province the following year.
nodes.src: Ibn Iyas; the Ottoman chronicles. Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.17–19; Seyyid Muradi and others.

nodes.label: The mutinies of the corps
nodes.full: The Ottoman regiments of Egypt rose again and again — over arrears of pay, debased coin, or a commander's death. In 1586 and 1589 the cavalry corps mutinied over pay; a general revolt in 1609 was crushed by Kara Mehmed Pasha in a campaign remembered as the 'second Ottoman conquest of Egypt'; and in 1711 a religious dispute set off nine months of fighting between the corps and the beys that wrecked quarters of Cairo. Between the mutinies the soldiers routinely deposed governors they disliked.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti and the earlier Ottoman-Egyptian chronicles (al-Damurdashi, al-Ishaqi). Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992) pp.34–41; Hathaway, The Politics of Households (1997).

nodes.label: The Faqari–Qasimi wars
nodes.full: Egypt's politics for nearly a century were structured by the feud between two Mamluk factional blocs, the Faqari (with white banners and the pomegranate emblem) and the Qasimi (red banners, disc emblem), which reached down into the villages and the guilds. Leaders were murdered at truce meetings; whole households were driven into exile or killed, the Faqari nearly annihilated in 1730. Neither the pasha nor the corps could stop it; the Qazdughli household finally absorbed the survivors of both.
nodes.src: P.M. Holt, 'The Beylicate in Ottoman Egypt' (1961); Hathaway, The Politics of Households (1997) and A Tale of Two Factions: Myth, Memory, and Identity in Ottoman Egypt and Yemen (2003).

nodes.label: Ali Bey's Syrian campaign
nodes.full: Ali Bey sent an Egyptian army north under Abu al-Dhahab and Isma'il Bey. It took Gaza and Jaffa, joined the Galilee shaykh Zahir al-Umar, beat the Ottoman governor of Damascus in the field, and entered the city in June 1771 — for a few days the Mamluks held both Cairo and Damascus. Then Abu al-Dhahab suddenly withdrew the whole army to Egypt, on a secret understanding with the Ottomans, and the campaign that had made Ali Bey a regional power collapsed.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti; the Ottoman and Damascene chronicles. Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.71–98; Thomas Philipp, Acre: The Rise and Fall of a Palestinian City 1730–1831 (2001).

nodes.label: The war of Ali Bey and Abu al-Dhahab
nodes.full: Driven from Cairo, Ali Bey took refuge with Zahir al-Umar at Acre, where a Russian naval squadron operating against the Ottomans in the eastern Mediterranean shelled Ottoman ports on his behalf and Beirut was briefly taken. In April 1773 he marched back toward Egypt, was ambushed and defeated by Abu al-Dhahab's forces at al-Salihiyya, wounded and captured, and died a week later in his rival's custody.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti; Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981) pp.99–120. The Russian dimension: A.I. Bagis and the Chesme-era literature.

nodes.label: The expedition of Hasan Pasha
nodes.full: In 1786 the Ottoman grand admiral Cezayirli Gazi Hasan Pasha landed with a fleet and army to break the beys and restore the tribute. He beat Murad Bey at al-Rahmaniyya, occupied Cairo, drove Ibrahim and Murad into Upper Egypt, cut taxes, and installed a compliant regime under Isma'il Bey. But when war with Russia broke out in 1787 he was recalled; within a year Ibrahim and Murad had returned, and the last Ottoman attempt to rule Egypt directly before Muhammad Ali was over.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti; Stanford Shaw, Between Old and New: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Selim III (1971) pp.242–52; Daniel Crecelius (ed.), Eighteenth Century Egypt: The Arabic Manuscript Sources (1990).

nodes.label: The Pyramids, Aboukir and the Cairo revolt
nodes.full: Bonaparte's infantry in squares broke Murad Bey's charging cavalry at Imbaba, opposite Cairo, on 21 July 1798 — the 'Battle of the Pyramids'. Ten days later Nelson annihilated the French fleet at anchor at Aboukir, trapping the army in Egypt. In October the population of Cairo rose against the occupiers, the fighting centring on al-Azhar; French artillery bombarded the mosque quarter, and the rising was crushed with mass executions. The occupation held on, isolated, until 1801.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, Muddat al-faransis bi-misr and 'Aja'ib al-athar. Henry Laurens, L'expédition d'Égypte (1989); Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007).

nodes.label: The eyalet and its offices
nodes.full: Egypt was governed on the standard Ottoman provincial template: a viceroy (pasha) with the rank of vizier, a council (divan), a chief Hanafi judge sent from Istanbul with a web of deputy qadis, a finance office keeping an annual budget, the seven military corps, and the obligation to remit a fixed tribute to the imperial treasury each year. The template stayed formally in place for 280 years even as the substance of power moved elsewhere.
nodes.src: Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization and Development of Ottoman Egypt 1517–1798 (1962) and the translated Ottoman Egypt in the Age of the French Revolution (1964). Winter, Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule (1992).

nodes.label: The iltizam tax-farm and the village
nodes.full: Direct state collection gave way to tax-farming: a multazim bought the right to collect a village's dues for a fixed payment plus recognised fees, kept the surplus, and held the farm for life and increasingly by inheritance. By the eighteenth century the beys, the ulama and Coptic financiers held most of the farms of Egypt, collecting through the village shaykh and the corvée, while the peasant's burden grew, the Bedouin took over whole districts, and villages emptied under the pressure.
nodes.src: Kenneth Cuno, The Pasha's Peasants: Land, Society, and Economy in Lower Egypt 1740–1858 (1992); Stanford Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization... (1962). The Hawwara of Upper Egypt: al-Jabarti.

nodes.label: Feeding Istanbul and the Holy Cities
nodes.full: Egypt owed the empire more than the cash tribute. It sent an annual shipment of grain and money for the poor of Mecca and Medina, outfitted and paid for the escort of the pilgrimage caravan, and its workshops wove the kiswa, the black embroidered covering of the Kaaba, renewed every year and carried to Mecca with the ceremonial camel-litter, the mahmal. Supplying the imperial capital with rice and beans was a further standing charge. These obligations were the price of the province's autonomy.
nodes.src: Suraiya Faroqhi, Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans (1994). Jane Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule 1516–1800 (2008) pp.55–58, 152–58.

nodes.label: The ulama as the notables of Cairo
nodes.full: The senior scholars of al-Azhar and the great mosques formed a self-perpetuating urban elite: they held tax farms and administered vast endowments, arbitrated between the rulers and the ruled, and spoke for the city in a crisis. In 1795, when Ibrahim and Murad Bey's new taxes provoked a shutdown of the markets, the shaykhs led the protest and extracted a written promise of relief. In the absence of any representative institution, the ulama were the nearest thing Egypt had to a civil society.
nodes.src: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, 'The Ulama of Cairo in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries', in Keddie (ed.), Scholars, Saints, and Sufis (1972). Gabriel Baer, 'Popular Revolt in Ottoman Cairo', Der Islam 54 (1977). Al-Jabarti, passim.

nodes.label: The guilds, the quarters and the market
nodes.full: The working city was organised in guilds — each trade a ta'ifa with its own shaykh, entry rules and internal court — and in residential quarters (harat), gated and closed at night under a headman and watchmen, sometimes with their own youth gangs. A market inspector (muhtasib) policed weights, prices and food quality. This dense fabric of small corporate bodies, rather than a municipal state, kept order in one of the world's largest cities.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Artisans et commerçants au Caire au XVIIIe siècle (1973) and Cairo (2000). Gabriel Baer, Egyptian Guilds in Modern Times (1964).

nodes.label: The waqf and the endowment economy
nodes.full: The religious endowment was everywhere. Rulers and merchants endowed mosques, drinking fountains (sabils), schools, hospitals and Sufi lodges, funding them from the rents of shops, houses, baths and farmland assigned in perpetuity. The 'family waqf' let an owner shelter property from the confiscations that regularly followed a bey's fall, drawing the income to his descendants as nominal administrators. A very large share of Cairo's real estate and much farmland was locked in waqf.
nodes.src: Daniel Crecelius, 'The Waqf of Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab', JESHO 34 (1991); Muhammad Afifi and the waqf-document scholarship. The registers of the Ministry of Awqaf, Cairo.

nodes.label: The sharia courts and their registers
nodes.full: Justice ran through a hierarchy of sharia courts — the chief court of the Bab al-'Ali and dozens of neighbourhood tribunals — whose scribes kept bound registers (sijills) of every deed, contract, marriage, divorce, inheritance and dispute they handled. All four Sunni legal schools had their own judges. Christians and Jews, entitled to their own communal courts, frequently chose the Muslim court instead for property and family matters, trusting its record-keeping. The registers are the richest source for Ottoman Egyptian society.
nodes.src: The Cairo court registers: studies by 'Abd al-Rahim 'Abd al-Rahman, Nelly Hanna, and Boğaç Ergene's methodological work. Nelly Hanna, Making Big Money in 1600: The Life and Times of Isma'il Abu Taqiyya (1998).

nodes.label: al-Azhar, the centre of the Sunni world
nodes.full: Under the Ottomans al-Azhar became the pre-eminent seat of Sunni learning anywhere. Students came from West Africa, the Maghrib, Syria, the Hijaz, Anatolia, India and the Malay world, housed and fed in residence halls (riwaqs) organised by homeland and legal school. Instruction was free, given in circles around individual shaykhs who issued personal licences to teach; the curriculum ran from grammar and logic to law, hadith and Qurʾanic science. The office of shaykh al-Azhar, its head, took shape in this period.
nodes.src: Bayard Dodge, Al-Azhar: A Millennium of Muslim Learning (1961); Jonathan Berkey, The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo (1992) for the earlier system; Rudolph Peters, 'Reinhard Schulze's Quest for an Islamic Enlightenment', Die Welt des Islams 30 (1990) on the debate about the period.

nodes.label: The Sufi orders and the great mawlids
nodes.full: Popular religion was organised by the Sufi brotherhoods — the Shadhiliyya, the Ahmadiyya of Sayyid al-Badawi, the Khalwatiyya, the Bakriyya whose head presided over the Cairo orders — with their lodges, litanies and public zikr. Their festivals were the largest gatherings in Egypt: the mawlid of al-Badawi at Tanta drew hundreds of thousands each autumn for a fair, a fair-ground and a religious carnival, and the Cairo mawlids of al-Husayn and al-Sayyida Zaynab filled whole quarters.
nodes.src: F. de Jong, Turuq and Turuq-Linked Institutions in Nineteenth Century Egypt (1978). The Tanta mawlid: J.W. McPherson, The Moulids of Egypt (1941); Edward Lane, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836) for the mature form.

nodes.label: The shrine city and the plague
nodes.full: Cairo was a landscape of holy tombs — the head-shrine of al-Husayn, the mosques of al-Sayyida Zaynab, al-Sayyida Nafisa and the imam al-Shafiʿi, and the inhabited 'cities of the dead' — and visiting them (ziyara) was everyday devotion. It became more so under the plague, which struck the city roughly every decade or two: the outbreak of 1791 is thought to have killed a fifth of Cairo. Debate on whether the faithful should flee an epidemic ran alongside processions with the Qurʾan and appeals to the saints.
nodes.src: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977) and the Ottoman-era continuation; Daniel Panzac, La peste dans l'Empire ottoman 1700–1850 (1985). Cairo's shrines: Caroline Williams, Islamic Monuments in Cairo (2008).

nodes.label: The Coptic Church in the Ottoman centuries
nodes.full: The Coptic Church reached its lowest point in numbers and wealth in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, then revived in the eighteenth as the archon families poured money into it: churches rebuilt, the desert monasteries restored, and a flourishing of icon painting led by the Armenian immigrant Yuhanna al-Armani and his Coptic partner Ibrahim al-Nasikh. The patriarch went on sending the metropolitan bishop to Ethiopia. From 1741 a small Coptic Catholic community formed under Franciscan influence.
nodes.src: Magdi Guirguis, An Armenian Artist in Ottoman Egypt: Yuhanna al-Armani and His Coptic Icons (2008); Febe Armanios, Coptic Christianity in Ottoman Egypt (2011).

nodes.label: The Jewish community of Ottoman Egypt
nodes.full: Egypt's Jews — Rabbanite and Karaite, with a layer of Iberian exiles and, later, North African and Italian traders — were self-governing under their own leaders, though the old office of nagid, head of all Egyptian Jewry, lapsed around the Ottoman conquest. In practice the community was often represented by whichever Jewish financier held the post of chief banker (sarraf) to the treasury or the customs. Numbers and wealth declined over the period; the storeroom of the Ben Ezra synagogue kept filling with discarded documents.
nodes.src: Jacob Landau, Jews in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (1969) for the later community; the Ottoman-era nagidate, Mark Cohen, Jewish Self-Government in Medieval Egypt (1980). The Geniza's long tail: S.D. Goitein.

nodes.label: The stirrings of reform
nodes.full: Late in the period new currents moved. Pilgrims returning from Arabia carried word of the austere Wahhabi movement then rising in Najd, which rejected the whole culture of shrines and Sufi orders. Within al-Azhar, revivalist teachers pressed for a return to the founding texts. And a handful of scholars, the young Hasan al-'Attar chief among them, sought out the French savants of the Institut d'Égypte after 1798 to learn their sciences — the first Egyptian intellectuals to treat European knowledge as something to acquire rather than dismiss.
nodes.src: Peter Gran, Islamic Roots of Capitalism: Egypt, 1760–1840 (1979) — the al-'Attar case. Al-Jabarti on the French Institut. The Wahhabi impact: Michael Cook and the Najdi sources.

nodes.label: Ottoman-Cairene architecture
nodes.full: Cairo's builders merged the imported Ottoman style — the slim pencil minaret, the single lead-covered dome, the blue Iznik tile — with the local Mamluk tradition of striped stone, stalactite portals and multi-part complexes. The domed mosque of Sinan Pasha at Bulaq (1571) and that of the sultan's mother Malika Safiyya (1610) are the Ottoman note; the sabil-kuttab, a marble drinking fountain below and a Qurʾan school for orphans above, became the signature charitable building on every important street corner.
nodes.src: Doris Behrens-Abouseif, Egypt's Adjustment to Ottoman Rule: Institutions, Waqf and Architecture in Cairo (1994). Caroline Williams, Islamic Monuments in Cairo: The Practical Guide (2008).

nodes.label: The courtyard houses of the elite
nodes.full: The wealthy of Ottoman Cairo lived in inward-facing courtyard houses whose public rooms — a tall, marble-floored reception hall (qaʿa) with a fountain, an upper loggia (maqʿad) catching the north wind, latticed mashrabiyya window screens — were designed for entertaining, shade and privacy. Bayt al-Suhaymi, grown by accretion over two centuries, and the palaces of the beys are the surviving examples of a domestic architecture perfectly adapted to the climate and the society.
nodes.src: Nelly Hanna, Habiter au Caire: la maison moyenne et ses habitants aux XVIIe et XVIIIe siècles (1991). Bernard Maury et al., Palais et maisons du Caire, vol.2: Époque ottomane (1983).

nodes.label: al-Jabarti's chronicle of the age
nodes.full: 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jabarti, an Azhar-trained scholar of a Yemeni family, wrote the 'Aja'ib al-athar — a year-by-year chronicle of events braided with obituaries of everyone of note, covering roughly 1688 to 1821 in dense, sharp, sometimes bitter detail. It is the essential narrative of the late Ottoman regime, the Mamluk beys, the French occupation and the rise of Muhammad Ali, and one of the last and greatest works of the classical Arabic historical tradition.
nodes.src: 'Abd al-Rahman al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar fi al-tarajim wa-al-akhbar: the Thomas Philipp & Moshe Perlmann annotated translation, 4 vols. (1994); the French-occupation portions translated by Shmuel Moreh, Napoleon in Egypt (1993).

nodes.label: The shadow play and the storytellers
nodes.full: Street entertainment carried the Mamluk inheritance forward: the khayal al-zill, a shadow-puppet theatre of translucent leather figures worked behind a lit screen, satirical, obscene and topical; the maddah reciting from the great popular epics — the deeds of 'Antar, of Baybars, of the Bani Hilal — over weeks in the coffee-houses; the mawlid tumblers, snake-charmers and rope-dancers; and the professional women singers and dancers, the 'awalim. Al-Jabarti and Edward Lane describe it all.
nodes.src: Edward Lane, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836) chs. 21–25. Shadow play: Paul Kahle, Zur Geschichte des arabischen Schattentheaters in Egypten (1909); the surviving Ibn Daniyal texts from the Mamluk period.

nodes.label: Cairo as a city of manuscripts
nodes.full: Egypt had no printing press until Bonaparte brought one in 1798, and the book meant the manuscript. Cairo was a major centre of copying and the book trade, with a booksellers' market by al-Azhar, guilds of scribes and illuminators, and great collections — the endowed libraries of the mosques and madrasas, and the private libraries of the beys and the ulama. Azhari scholarship itself took the form of commentaries and marginal glosses copied and re-copied around a core of canonical texts.
nodes.src: Nelly Hanna, In Praise of Books: A Cultural History of Cairo's Middle Class, Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century (2003). Ekmeleddin İhsanoğlu on the delayed adoption of print.

nodes.label: The takht and the sung poem
nodes.full: Arabic art music in Egypt was performed by the small takht ensemble — lute (ʿud), plucked zither (qanun), reed flute (nay), tambourine (riqq) — playing a suite (wasla) of instrumental and vocal pieces held together by a single melodic mode. Alongside it ran the colloquial sung poetry of the mawwal, the strophic muwashshah, the Sufi lodges' hymnody, and the highly developed art of Qurʾanic recitation. It is the tradition from which modern Egyptian music grew.
nodes.src: A.J. Racy, Making Music in the Arab World: The Culture and Artistry of Tarab (2003). The Ottoman-era repertoire is reconstructed from 19th-century notations; Edward Lane, Modern Egyptians, ch. 18.

nodes.label: The Azhari sciences and the commentary tradition
nodes.full: Learning at al-Azhar was divided between the 'transmitted' sciences — Qurʾan, hadith, jurisprudence and their auxiliaries — and the 'rational' ones — Arabic grammar, logic, rhetoric, and enough arithmetic and astronomy to fix the calendar and the prayer times. Scholarship proceeded by writing commentaries and glosses on a settled body of authoritative texts. Whether this was intellectual stagnation or the normal working of a mature tradition is one of the sharpest debates in the field.
nodes.src: The 'decline' debate: Peter Gran, Islamic Roots of Capitalism (1979) argues against it; Reinhard Schulze; Ahmad Dallal, Islam without Europe: Traditions of Reform in Eighteenth-Century Islamic Thought (2018). Al-Jabarti's own scholarly biography of his teachers.

nodes.label: The chroniclers of the corps and the households
nodes.full: Before al-Jabarti, Ottoman Egypt produced a rich vernacular historiography written largely by and for the military class — Ahmad Shalabi's 'Awdah al-isharat, the cluster of anonymous 'Damurdashi' chronicles, al-Ishaqi's earlier work — recounting the mutinies, the factional wars and the rise and fall of the beys in a plain, sometimes colloquial Arabic quite unlike the ornate Ottoman court style. It is a distinctively Egyptian tradition of contemporary history from the ground up.
nodes.src: Daniel Crecelius (ed.), Eighteenth Century Egypt: The Arabic Manuscript Sources (1990); P.M. Holt, 'Al-Jabarti's Introduction to the History of Ottoman Egypt', BSOAS 25 (1962). The Damurdashi chronicles: ed. Daniel Crecelius & 'Abd al-Wahhab Bakr (1991).

nodes.label: Medicine, the druggist and the plague
nodes.full: Egyptian medicine worked within the Galenic and Ibn Sina tradition, taught from the classic texts and practised by learned physicians, barber-surgeons, bonesetters and the druggists (ʿattarin) of the great spice bazaar. The Mamluk-era Mansuri hospital still functioned, much decayed. Plague was the central medical problem, and the tension between a doctrine of contagion and one of divine decree ran through the debate. The French army's physicians, arriving in 1798, were the first sustained contact with a different medical world.
nodes.src: Nancy Gallagher, Medicine and Power in Tunisia (1983) for the regional picture; LaVerne Kuhnke, Lives at Risk: Public Health in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (1990) for the transition. Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977).

nodes.label: Two calendars and the hours of prayer
nodes.full: Egypt ran on two calendars at once: the Islamic lunar one for religious life, and the Coptic solar calendar — a survival of the ancient Egyptian year — still used for the agricultural seasons, the flood, and much of the tax accounting, its new year (Nawruz) marked by festivities. Mosque timekeepers (muwaqqits) computed the five daily prayer times by the sun and by instruments, the astrolabe and the sundial were still made and used, and the Nilometer criers announced the river.
nodes.src: David King, In Synchrony with the Heavens: Studies in Astronomical Timekeeping and Instrumentation in Medieval Islamic Civilization (2004–05). The Coptic calendar's persistence: Alfred Butler and the modern Egyptian farmers' almanac tradition.

nodes.label: The French savants and the Description de l'Égypte
nodes.full: Bonaparte's expedition brought a Commission of some 160 scholars — mathematicians, engineers, naturalists, orientalists, artists — who founded the Institut d'Égypte in a requisitioned Cairo palace and set about surveying the country's antiquities, geography, natural history and present state. Soldiers repairing a fort at Rosetta turned up the trilingual stone that would crack the hieroglyphs. The huge Description de l'Égypte, published over 1809–1829, and Champollion's decipherment of 1822 launched the modern European study of Egypt.
nodes.src: Description de l'Égypte (Paris, 1809–1829). Yves Laissus, L'Égypte, une aventure savante 1798–1801 (1998); Nina Burleigh, Mirage: Napoleon's Scientists and the Unveiling of Egypt (2007). Al-Jabarti's visit to the Institut.

nodes.label: The Yemeni coffee boom
nodes.full: For nearly two centuries Egypt's commercial life turned on coffee. The Yemeni crop was shipped from Mocha to Jidda, ferried across to Suez, and carried by camel to Cairo, where the great coffee merchants — some of the richest men in the Ottoman world — redistributed it to Anatolia, the Balkans, the Maghrib and, from the seventeenth century, Europe. The coffee-house itself spread out of Egypt and the Hijaz. The trade collapsed when cheap Caribbean and Javanese coffee undercut Yemen after about 1720.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Artisans et commerçants au Caire au XVIIIe siècle (1973), vol.1; Michel Tuchscherer (ed.), Le commerce du café avant l'ère des plantations coloniales (2001); Ralph Hattox, Coffee and Coffeehouses (1985).

nodes.label: The transit trade and the Red Sea
nodes.full: Beyond coffee, Indian textiles, pepper and other spices, and pilgrims' goods continued to move up the Red Sea to Suez and across to Cairo, handled by a class of 'India merchants', and Egyptian rice, grain, sugar, natron and linen went out through Alexandria and Damietta. The Cape route and the Persian Gulf took a growing share over the period, and the volume fell, but the Cairo–Suez transit remained a real and profitable economy — one reason Egypt was worth invading.
nodes.src: Raymond, Artisans et commerçants (1973); Colette Establet & Jean-Paul Pascual on the Damascus and Cairo merchant inventories; Giancarlo Casale, The Ottoman Age of Exploration (2010) on the Red Sea policy.

nodes.label: The workshops of Cairo
nodes.full: Cairo in the eighteenth century still had a large manufacturing sector — sugar refineries, textile weaving and dyeing, tanning, soap and oil-pressing, arms and the famous sword-cutlers, metal and leather work — organised in guilds and supplied through the courtyard warehouses (wikalas). It produced for Egypt, for the Ottoman markets, and for the pilgrimage traffic. André Raymond's reconstruction from the estate inventories shows a working urban economy of real depth, not a city living only on transit.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Artisans et commerçants au Caire au XVIIIe siècle, 2 vols. (1973) — the foundational study, built from thousands of probate inventories in the court registers.

nodes.label: The land, the crops and the multazims
nodes.full: Egyptian agriculture kept its ancient shape — wheat, beans and barley on the flooded basins, rice and later maize in the Delta, sugarcane and indigo in the south, flax for the linen trade — worked by the fallahin and taxed through the multazims. The surplus fed Egypt, the Holy Cities and Istanbul and was exported. The eighteenth century saw commercial pressures grow: heavier assessment, the spread of maize, and, in some Delta districts, the beginnings of production for the market rather than subsistence.
nodes.src: Kenneth Cuno, The Pasha's Peasants: Land, Society, and Economy in Lower Egypt 1740–1858 (1992); Alan Richards, Egypt's Agricultural Development 1800–1980 (1982) for the baseline.

nodes.label: The mint, the para and the money-changers
nodes.full: Egypt struck its own version of the Ottoman small silver coin, the para or medin, at a mint in the Citadel that the Janissary corps controlled and milked. Recurrent debasement — cutting the silver to skim a profit — set off market shutdowns and riots. Large transactions used European silver, the Spanish real and later the Maria Theresa thaler, and the credit system ran on the money-changers (sarrafs), a trade largely in Coptic and Jewish hands, who financed the tax farms and the merchants.
nodes.src: Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000); Raymond, Artisans et commerçants (1973) on the sarrafs and the money riots.

nodes.label: The fiscal drain and the impoverished province
nodes.full: By the late eighteenth century Egypt's wealth was being pumped out faster than it was made. The tribute still went to Istanbul; the beys' households consumed vast sums on troops, weapons and display; every change of regime brought confiscations and forced loans on the merchants and the ulama; and Ibrahim and Murad Bey layered on new taxes and monopolies. Al-Jabarti's chronicle of these years is a litany of exactions, ruined merchants, and a countryside falling out of cultivation.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar for 1775–98. André Raymond, 'The Economic Crisis of Egypt in the Eighteenth Century', in Udovitch (ed.), The Islamic Middle East 700–1900 (1981).

nodes.label: The wikala, the sabil and the water supply
nodes.full: A great commercial city ran without a municipal utility. Merchants and their goods were housed in the wikala — a fortified courtyard block with warehouses on the ground floor and lodgings above. Water came from the Nile by aqueduct to Citadel cisterns, and otherwise by tens of thousands of water-carriers with skins, distributed at the endowed public fountains (sabils). Baths, mills and the water-lifting saqiya completed a working infrastructure built entirely from private endowment.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Cairo (2000) pp.189–232; Behrens-Abouseif, Egypt's Adjustment to Ottoman Rule (1994). The water-carriers: Edward Lane, Modern Egyptians, ch. 14.

nodes.label: Textile, dye and sugar technology
nodes.full: Pre-industrial manufacture worked at a substantial scale. The drawloom produced figured cloth; the dye-houses used indigo, safflower and madder in stone vats; and in the sugar towns of Upper Egypt the boiling-houses (masabik) crushed cane in ox-mills, boiled the juice in copper pans, and set it to crystallise and drain in clay cones — a technology essentially unchanged since the Middle Ages and still competitive on Ottoman and Mediterranean markets.
nodes.src: Sato Tsugitaka, Sugar in the Social Life of Medieval Islam (2015) for the technique's continuity; Raymond, Artisans et commerçants (1973) on the Cairo dye and cloth trades.

nodes.label: The firearm and the Mamluk who would not use it
nodes.full: The single decisive military-technology story of the period is one of refusal. The Mamluk cavalry despised the handgun as a weapon unfit for a horseman, and lost the empire to Ottoman guns and muskets in 1516–17. Under the Ottomans the beys' households went on fighting mainly with lance, sabre and composite bow, keeping their reputation as superb cavalry while their army fell two centuries behind. In 1798 that army charged Bonaparte's musket-and-bayonet infantry squares and was destroyed in an hour.
nodes.src: David Ayalon, Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom: A Challenge to a Mediaeval Society (1956, 2nd ed. 1978). The 1798 encounter: al-Jabarti; Juan Cole, Napoleon's Egypt (2007).

nodes.label: The Nile as the country's highway
nodes.full: Almost all bulk movement in Egypt went by river. Grain, sugar, stone, coffee and passengers travelled in the broad-sailed dahabiyya and the cargo qayasa, running south on the prevailing north wind and north on the current, in a seasonal rhythm set by wind and flood. The First Cataract at Aswan sealed the southern end; the Delta canals, silting for want of dredging, were the weak points. The boat was the circulatory system of a 1,000-kilometre-long country.
nodes.src: John Cooper, The Medieval Nile: Route, Navigation, and Landscape in Islamic Egypt (2014) for the technique's long continuity; the Description de l'Égypte, 'État moderne', on the boats of 1798.

nodes.label: Cairo, the crossroads of three trade worlds
nodes.full: Cairo joined three great commercial systems: the Mediterranean, reached through Alexandria and Rosetta and Damietta; the Red Sea and India, through Suez; and the caravan routes to the Sudan, Darfur and the Maghrib. Coffee, spices, Indian and European textiles, Sudanese gold, gum, ivory, ostrich feathers and slaves passed through it, handled by distinct merchant communities — Maghribi, Syrian, Hijazi, Indian, Sudanese — each with its own warehouses. It was one of the world's half-dozen great emporia.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Cairo (2000) and Artisans et commerçants (1973). Terence Walz, Trade between Egypt and Bilad as-Sudan 1700–1820 (1978).

nodes.label: The hajj caravan and the Holy Cities
nodes.full: Cairo assembled the largest of the pilgrimage caravans — tens of thousands of people and animals gathering each year for the desert crossing to Mecca under the amir al-hajj, escorted by troops, preceded by the ceremonial camel-litter (mahmal) and carrying the new kiswa for the Kaaba and the charity money for the Holy Cities. The caravan was a moving fair, a source of prestige for whoever commanded it, and a highway for news, goods, disease and — late in the period — the ideas of the Wahhabi movement.
nodes.src: Suraiya Faroqhi, Pilgrims and Sultans: The Hajj under the Ottomans 1517–1683 (1994). The Egyptian caravan: Jane Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule (2008); al-Jabarti's annual notices.

nodes.label: The Forty Days Road and the Sudan trade
nodes.full: The Darb al-Arbaʿin, the 'Forty Days Road', ran from the sultanate of Darfur across the desert to Asyut in Upper Egypt, bringing slaves, ivory, gum arabic, ostrich feathers, tamarind, natron and camels north in large annual caravans handled by the Jallaba merchants. Slaves came into Egypt in numbers from the Sudan and further afield — for domestic service, for the military households, and for agricultural labour in the south — a trade that grew through the eighteenth century.
nodes.src: Terence Walz, Trade between Egypt and Bilad as-Sudan 1700–1820 (1978). Rex O'Fahey, State and Society in Dar Fur (1980). The slave trade: Gabriel Baer, 'Slavery in Nineteenth Century Egypt', Journal of African History 8 (1967) for the continuation.

nodes.label: The European merchants and the capitulations
nodes.full: French and English trading 'nations', with resident consuls and the tax and legal privileges granted by the Ottoman capitulations, operated at Cairo and the ports through the whole period — the French of Marseille the largest, buying coffee, textiles, drugs, gum, rice and natron and selling woollens and silver. The trade was often difficult and the merchants harassed by the beys, but the European commercial foothold was long established by the time the French army arrived to make it a political one.
nodes.src: Robert Paris, Histoire du commerce de Marseille, vol.5: Le Levant (1957). Daniel Panzac, La caravane maritime: marins européens et marchands ottomans en Méditerranée 1680–1830 (2004).

nodes.label: Egypt in the Ottoman empire
nodes.full: Egypt was a central province of the empire, not a margin. It sent the largest single tribute, provisioned the capital and the Holy Cities, supplied troops and grain for the sultan's wars, and received governors, judges and garrison regiments from Istanbul. Its beys eyed Syria and the Hijaz; its households recruited from the same Caucasus as the sultan's; its scholars and Sufi networks reached across the whole Ottoman and Muslim world. The empire's problems and Egypt's were the same problems.
nodes.src: Jane Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule 1516–1800 (2008); Suraiya Faroqhi (ed.), The Cambridge History of Turkey, vol.3 (2006).

nodes.label: 1798 and the Eastern Question
nodes.full: Bonaparte's expedition dragged Egypt into the European state system. Britain, seeing a threat to the route to India, brought the Royal Navy, subsidised an Ottoman counter-attack, and made Egypt's future a matter of great-power concern. The Ottoman–Russian–British coalition that expelled the French, and the treaties that followed, treated Egypt as a strategic prize. The 'Eastern Question' — what the powers would do about the Ottoman empire's weakness — had opened, with Egypt near its centre.
nodes.src: Henry Laurens, L'expédition d'Égypte 1798–1801 (1989) and Le royaume impossible: la France et la genèse du monde arabe (1990). Edward Ingram, Britain's Persian Connection 1798–1828 (1992).

nodes.label: Cairo among the world's great cities
nodes.full: With something like a quarter of a million people, Cairo was one of the largest cities on earth outside China. It had lost the status of an imperial capital but kept the scale: the dense walled medieval core with its bazaars and monuments, the Nile port of Bulaq handling the river trade, the older Fustat to the south, and the fashionable Azbakiyya district around a seasonal lake where the beys built their palaces and gardens. A European visitor in 1798 still found it a metropolis of the first rank.
nodes.src: André Raymond, Cairo (2000) — the population estimate and the topography. The Description de l'Égypte, 'État moderne', with its great map of 1798.

nodes.label: The Nile, the famines and the plague
nodes.full: Egyptian demography swung violently with the river and the epidemic. A failed flood meant famine within the year, and the great dearth of 1784–1785, worsened by plague and misrule, is thought to have killed something like a sixth of the population. Plague itself returned every decade or two through the whole period, the 1791 outbreak carrying off perhaps a fifth of Cairo. Between the disasters the population recovered; the trend line is hard to read, but it did not grow.
nodes.src: Daniel Panzac, La peste dans l'Empire ottoman 1700–1850 (1985) and 'The Population of Egypt in the Nineteenth Century', Asian and African Studies 21 (1987). Al-Jabarti on the 1784–85 famine.

nodes.label: The Bedouin and the retreat of settled power
nodes.full: As the Ottoman-Mamluk state weakened, the Bedouin gained ground. In Upper Egypt the Hawwara confederation ruled whole provinces as near-independent lords, collecting the taxes and leading their own troops; the ʿArab of the eastern and western deserts controlled the trade routes and raided the cultivation at will. The beys of Cairo alternately fought and allied with them, but could not hold the country's margins, which slid out of any effective government.
nodes.src: Al-Jabarti, passim, on the Hawwara. Muhammad Sabry and the Upper Egypt material; Nelly Hanna, State and Society in Mamluk and Ottoman Egypt for the longer trajectory.

nodes.label: Egypt seen by the travellers
nodes.full: A growing shelf of European travel books described Egypt for outside readers — Richard Pococke and Frederik Norden in the 1730s–40s, Carsten Niebuhr, Claude-Étienne Savary, and above all Constantin-François Volney, whose Voyage en Égypte et en Syrie of 1787 argued that a rich, ill-governed Egypt could be taken by a small European force and that its conquest would command the route to India. Bonaparte read it closely; it helped make the invasion thinkable.
nodes.src: C.-F. Volney, Voyage en Syrie et en Égypte (1787). Pococke, A Description of the East (1743–45); Norden, Voyage d'Égypte et de Nubie (1755). Henry Laurens, Les origines intellectuelles de l'expédition d'Égypte (1987).

nodes.label: Ali Bey al-Kabir
nodes.full: Ali Bey was a Georgian priest's son, seized as a boy and sold into the Qazdughli household in Cairo, where he rose by nerve and violence to be shaykh al-balad and then something close to an independent sovereign — expelling Ottoman governors, minting his own coin, dreaming of restoring a Mamluk empire in Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz. He was undone by the men he had raised and freed: his lieutenant Abu al-Dhahab turned on him, and he died of his wounds in his rival's camp, the last of the would-be Mamluk kings.
nodes.src: Daniel Crecelius, The Roots of Modern Egypt (1981). The near-contemporary European life: [S. Lusignan], A History of the Revolt of Ali Bey (1783), to be used with caution.

nodes.label: al-Jabarti, the watcher of the age
nodes.full: Al-Jabarti came from a scholarly family with property and standing, trained at al-Azhar, and was appointed to the consultative council the French set up — service that later drew criticism, and that gave him a close view of the occupiers he wrote about with such disdain. He spent four decades on his chronicle, through the French years, the anarchy that followed, and Muhammad Ali's rise, losing a son to political violence along the way. His unsparing eye is the lens through which the period is seen.
nodes.src: Thomas Philipp & Guido Schwald (eds.), Abd al-Rahman al-Jabarti's History of Egypt (1994), including the biographical introduction. David Ayalon, 'The Historian al-Jabarti and His Background', BSOAS 23 (1960).

nodes.label: The Cairo merchant
nodes.full: The court registers let a Cairo merchant's whole career be reconstructed — a man like Ismaʿil Abu Taqiyya, who dealt in Yemeni coffee and Indian spices, built up a portfolio of houses, shops and rural tax-farms, ran agents from the Red Sea to Venice, financed other traders, endowed a mosque, and married into the military elite. Such men were a substantial urban bourgeoisie, neither courtiers nor guildsmen, whose wealth and connections gave Ottoman Cairo much of its economic depth.
nodes.src: Nelly Hanna, Making Big Money in 1600: The Life and Times of Isma'il Abu Taqiyya, Egyptian Merchant (1998).

nodes.label: The multazim and the fallah
nodes.full: The rural order had two ends. At one was the multazim — a bey, an army officer, an Azhar shaykh, a Coptic financier — who held the right to a village's taxes and drew its surplus through the local shaykh. At the other was the fallah household, working a plot on the flooded basin, turning the saqiya, owing labour on the dykes, and bearing the assessment, the fees, the requisitions and, in a bad year, the collector's whip. The Description de l'Égypte and the court records document both.
nodes.src: Kenneth Cuno, The Pasha's Peasants (1992); Kenneth Cuno & Michael Reimer, 'The Census Registers of Nineteenth-Century Egypt', Journal of Egyptian History (2010) for the method. The Description, 'État moderne'.

nodes.label: The women of the households
nodes.full: The women of the Mamluk and Ottoman elite are glimpsed mainly through endowment deeds and court cases, and some were considerable figures. A bey's widow like Shawikar Qadin, who married in turn several of the most powerful men of the seventeenth century, commanded her own wealth, household and patronage and acted in politics in her own right. Elite women routinely held property, founded waqfs, sued and were sued, and the marriage of a grandee's daughter or freedwoman cemented alliances between households.
nodes.src: Jane Hathaway, The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt (1997) on Shawikar and the household women; Mary Ann Fay, 'Women and Waqf: Property, Power, and the Domain of Gender in Eighteenth-Century Egypt', in Zilfi (ed.), Women in the Ottoman Empire (1997).

nodes.label: Yuhanna al-Armani, the icon painter
nodes.full: Yuhanna al-Armani was an Armenian who settled in Cairo and, with his Coptic partner Ibrahim al-Nasikh, ran the workshop that supplied hundreds of icons to the churches and monasteries of the eighteenth-century Coptic revival. An unusual survival of his commission contracts and a household account book lets a Christian artisan's working life — his patrons, his prices, his materials, his rented house — be followed in detail, a rare individual portrait from below the elite.
nodes.src: Magdi Guirguis, An Armenian Artist in Ottoman Egypt: Yuhanna al-Armani and His Coptic Icons (2008).
